Yamaha/Roland synthesizer technical documentation (program/part level parameters)

fields.definition: The momentary audio artifact — a click, gap, or abrupt jump in level or timbre — that can occur at the instant a synthesizer switches to a new patch, typically triggered by a MIDI Program (or Bank) Change, when currently held notes are cut off or the incoming patch's level and envelope state differ from the outgoing one.
fields.plain_english: The little glitch, pop, or sudden change in loudness you sometimes hear right when a synth jumps to a new sound.
fields.purpose_function: Recognising this transient matters because it can intrude on a live performance or a recording; understanding what causes it guides players and sound designers in switching sounds without an audible glitch.
fields.practical_application: To avoid patch-change transients on stage, a keyboardist changes programs during rests, uses a synth's seamless/gapless sound-transition feature, or keeps a sustaining part on a separate layer while switching the other.
common_mistakes: Changing patches while notes are still held, which cuts them off audibly in the middle of a phrase
Assuming the click is a hardware fault rather than a normal consequence of the switch and of level/envelope differences between patches
Not enabling a synth's seamless or gapless patch-change mode when the instrument provides one
scenario_contexts: A live keyboard player switching between song sections hears the held chord cut off at the program change
Building a set list so that program changes land on rests rather than under sustained notes
Editing a MIDI mock-up where a mid-note program change leaves an audible glitch in the render

sources: MIDI Association, MIDI 1.0 Detailed Specification (Program Change, Bank Select)
Roland/Korg synthesizer technical documentation (seamless/gapless sound-transition and sound-hold features)

fields.definition: In a pipe (or electronic) organ, the division of the instrument played from the pedalboard with the feet, having its own set of stops and ranks and typically supplying the low bass foundation of the instrument.
fields.plain_english: The part of an organ the player controls with the feet on a large footboard of keys; it usually plays the deep bass notes and has its own set of pipe sounds.
fields.purpose_function: It exists so the organist can play an independent bass line with the feet while the hands play the manuals, and it houses the large low-pitched stops that give the organ its deep foundation.
fields.practical_application: When recording an organ, the engineer chooses low-frequency-capable microphones and monitoring to capture the pedal division's very low fundamentals (a 16' or 32' stop can extend well below 32 Hz) while managing room modes and structural rumble.
common_mistakes: Confusing the pedal division (played by the feet) with a manual (played by the hands)
Assuming the pedal division always sounds the lowest octave, when its pitch depends on which stops (8', 16', 32') are drawn
Specifying microphones or monitors that cannot reproduce the 16' and 32' pedal fundamentals, so the true low end is never heard
scenario_contexts: Recording a large pipe organ and capturing the pedal division's sub-bass in a reverberant space
Reinforcing an organ recital where a 32' pedal stop challenges the PA's low-frequency headroom
Reviewing an organ mix to confirm the pedal line is present and not lost to room rumble or filtering

sources: Audsley, The Art of Organ Building
Grove Dictionary of Music and Musicians (organ; divisions and pedal organ)

fields.definition: A concert harp fitted with seven pedals — one for each note name — that, through a double-action mechanism, mechanically shorten the sounding strings to raise each pitch class by a semitone (flat, natural, or sharp), enabling the diatonically strung instrument to play in all keys.
fields.plain_english: The large orchestral harp with seven foot pedals; each pedal retunes all the strings of one note (all the C's, all the D's, and so on) up or down a semitone so the player can play in any key.
fields.purpose_function: The pedal mechanism exists to give a diatonically strung harp full chromatic capability without adding strings, letting one instrument produce the sharps and flats of every key.
fields.practical_application: When recording a pedal harp, engineers place microphones to balance the bright attack near the soundboard against the body's resonance, and must account for audible mechanical pedal and action noise during quiet passages.
common_mistakes: Confusing the pedal (concert) harp with the lever (folk/Celtic) harp, which changes pitch with hand-operated levers rather than pedals
Thinking each pedal changes only one string, when a pedal changes every string of that note name across all octaves
Failing to plan for mechanical pedal-mechanism noise, which close mics readily capture in quiet passages
scenario_contexts: Miking a solo concert harp for a classical recording
Placing the harp in an orchestral session and managing bleed from adjacent sections
Troubleshooting audible pedal or action clicks captured during a quiet studio take

sources: Fletcher & Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments
Adler, The Study of Orchestration
Grove Dictionary of Music and Musicians (harp)

fields.definition: The electrical switching convention — normally-open or normally-closed — by which a sustain or footswitch pedal signals its pressed and released states to a keyboard or module, and the matching 'pedal polarity' setting on the instrument that ensures the pedal is interpreted the correct way round.
fields.plain_english: Whether a foot pedal's switch is 'open' or 'closed' when you step on it. If the keyboard's polarity setting does not match the pedal, sustain works backwards — notes hold when your foot is off and stop when you press.
fields.purpose_function: The setting exists because sustain pedals from different makers use opposite switching conventions; matching the polarity lets any pedal operate correctly instead of inverted.
fields.practical_application: When a newly connected sustain pedal behaves backwards, a technician sets the keyboard's pedal-polarity parameter, or connects the pedal before power-up so the instrument's auto-detect reads the correct rest state.
common_mistakes: Assuming a backwards-working pedal is faulty, when it is actually a polarity mismatch between pedal and keyboard
Hot-plugging the pedal after power-on so the instrument's auto-detect latches the wrong rest state — connect the pedal before switching on when relying on auto-detect
Confusing pedal polarity (a switch convention) with audio signal polarity or phase in cable wiring
scenario_contexts: A guest keyboardist's third-party sustain pedal sustains inverted on the house synth
Configuring a stage keyboard rig so every pedal behaves consistently before a show
Setting the polarity parameter on a digital piano after switching to a different-brand pedal

sources: Roland/Yamaha keyboard owner's and technical manuals (pedal/damper polarity setting)
MIDI Association, MIDI 1.0 Detailed Specification (CC 64 Damper/Sustain)

fields.definition: The bright, brilliant, penetrating timbral quality characteristic of the piccolo — the small transverse flute pitched an octave above the concert flute — arising from its high playing register and the strong high-frequency content of its spectrum.
fields.plain_english: The piccolo's very high, whistle-like, cutting tone that easily rides on top of a full band or orchestra.
fields.purpose_function: This brightness lets the piccolo project above large ensembles and add sparkle to the top of the texture, which is why it is used to reinforce and brighten the highest melodic lines.
fields.practical_application: When recording or mixing piccolo, engineers manage its brightness and high output level with suitable mic placement (backed off and slightly off-axis from the embouchure) and gentle high-frequency control to avoid harsh, sibilant peaks.
common_mistakes: Placing a mic directly in front of the embouchure hole, capturing excessive breath noise and a harsh, over-bright tone
Boosting high frequencies on an already-bright piccolo and pushing it into harshness

UNSAFE: monitoring a close-mic'd piccolo at high levels without hearing protection — its high-SPL output concentrated in the ear-sensitive 2–4 kHz region can contribute to hearing damage over long sessions (OSHA 29 CFR 1910.95)
scenario_contexts: Recording piccolo doublings in a wind ensemble where it must sit brightly above the flutes
Taming a harsh piccolo in a film-score mix with de-essing and gentle EQ
Positioning microphones in an orchestral session to balance piccolo brilliance against the rest of the woodwinds

sources: Adler, The Study of Orchestration
Fletcher & Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments (flutes and the piccolo)

fields.definition: In a pipe organ, a rank is a complete set of pipes of uniform construction and tone colour, arranged one pipe per note across the compass of a keyboard; drawing a stop brings one rank — or, in the case of a mixture, several ranks — into play.
fields.plain_english: A rank is one full row of organ pipes that all share the same sound, with a separate pipe for every key; pulling a stop turns a rank on.
fields.purpose_function: Ranks organise an organ's pipes into consistent voices so that each stop selects a distinct timbre; combining ranks builds up the instrument's overall tone and volume.
fields.practical_application: When recording or documenting an organ, technicians identify ranks by their stop names and pitch length (for example an 8' Principal) to understand the tonal and spatial layout of the pipes being captured.
common_mistakes: Confusing a rank (a set of pipes) with a stop (the control that brings ranks into play), when one stop can draw more than one rank in a mixture
Assuming one rank equals one pipe, when a rank has one pipe per note across the whole keyboard
Misreading pitch designations (8', 4', 2') as pipe counts, when they describe the sounding pitch of the rank
scenario_contexts: Cataloguing an organ's stop list before a recording session
Spot-miking individual ranks or divisions on a large instrument
Discussing with an organ builder which ranks contribute unwanted mechanical or wind noise

sources: Audsley, The Art of Organ Building
Grove Dictionary of Music and Musicians (organ; rank and stop)

fields.definition: The brief, tonally complex onset that occurs as an organ pipe begins to sound ('speaks'), before it settles into steady tone — often including a transient 'chiff' of noise and momentarily unstable harmonics that is characteristic of the pipe's voicing.
fields.plain_english: The small burst of sound an organ pipe makes at the very start of a note, before it settles into its steady tone — sometimes heard as a soft 'chiff.'
fields.purpose_function: The speech transient is central to how a pipe's onset is heard and recognised; voicers deliberately shape it to give a rank its characteristic attack and clarity.
fields.practical_application: When recording an organ, engineers preserve these onset transients with fast, transient-accurate microphones and minimal limiting, since over-compression or slow-settling capture blurs the pipe's articulation.
common_mistakes: Treating the speech transient as noise to be removed, when it is an intrinsic and musically important part of a pipe's tone
Confusing 'speech' (the onset of tone) with the pipe's steady-state sound
Applying heavy limiting or slow-attack processing that smears the transient and robs the organ of articulation
scenario_contexts: Choosing microphones and preamps that preserve fast onset transients when recording a tracker organ
Evaluating a sampled organ library for realistic pipe speech and attack behaviour
Discussing voicing and regulation of chiff with an organ builder

sources: Fletcher & Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments (organ pipes; attack transients)
Audsley, The Art of Organ Building (speech and voicing)

fields.definition: A performance technique on bowed string instruments in which the player plucks the strings with a finger (or occasionally the thumb) instead of drawing the bow across them, producing a short, percussive, quickly decaying note.
fields.plain_english: Instead of using the bow, the player plucks the strings with a fingertip, like plucking a guitar, giving a short, punchy note that fades fast.
fields.purpose_function: It provides a contrasting articulation to bowed (arco) playing, offering a percussive, rhythmic, quickly decaying sound; it is one of the core expressive techniques of the string family.
fields.practical_application: When recording strings, an engineer captures the fast attack and short decay of pizzicato with close or spot mics, and avoids the heavy compression that would kill its natural transient and quick decay.
common_mistakes: Confusing pizzicato with staccato — pizzicato means plucking the string, while staccato is a short articulation that can be played either arco or pizzicato
Assuming pizzicato applies to only one instrument, when it is used across the whole bowed-string family (violin, viola, cello, double bass)
Over-compressing pizzicato in the mix, which flattens the fast attack and quick decay that define the sound
scenario_contexts: Tracking a string quartet where the cellist alternates between arco and pizzicato passages
A film-score session requiring tight, rhythmic pizzicato from the double-bass section
Editing a sampled-string MIDI part that switches to a pizzicato articulation via a keyswitch

sources: Adler, The Study of Orchestration
Piston, Orchestration
Grove Dictionary of Music and Musicians (pizzicato)
